summary: This standards-track memo describes how to use the RSASSA-PSS digital signature algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), the format used to sign and encrypt messages and data. It is a companion to the certificate conventions in RFC 4055.

eli5.summary: This document explains how to use a modern kind of digital signature to protect signed messages and files.

subtitle: How to sign CMS messages with the RSASSA-PSS signature scheme, and which parameters must match.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needed a defined way to carry RSASSA-PSS signatures, a signature scheme built on mathematical foundations rather than the ad hoc PKCS #1 v1.5 design.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says which algorithm identifiers to use in certificates and signatures, how the hash function must line up across the signed-data fields, and which certificate parameters must be checked against the signature parameters.
tldr.outcome: Verifiers must fail validation if the certificate and signature parameters disagree. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What This RFC Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 4056 sets the conventions for using the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) with the CMS signed-data content type. CMS values are generated using ASN.1, with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).

The document is written to be used together with RFC 4055. All of the ASN.1 structures it refers to are defined there. The RSASSA-PSS algorithm itself is defined in RFC 3447, and CMS in RFC 3852.
sections.eli5: This is a short instruction sheet for using one particular kind of digital seal inside signed messages. The details of the seal live in other documents.

sections.title: Why Use the PSS Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC notes that there are no known defects with the older PKCS #1 v1.5 signature algorithm. RSASSA-PSS was developed anyway, to have more mathematically provable security.

The contrast it draws is about origin: PKCS #1 v1.5 signatures were developed in an ad hoc manner, while RSASSA-PSS was developed based on mathematical foundations.
sections.eli5: The old seal was invented by trial and error and worked fine. The new one was designed from math so that people can prove it is strong.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
For RSA public keys in certificates, two algorithm identifiers can be used: rsaEncryption ({ pkcs-1 1 }) and id-RSASSA-PSS ({ pkcs-1 10 }). With rsaEncryption, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST contain NULL. With id-RSASSA-PSS, the parameters field MUST either be absent or contain RSASSA-PSS-params.

In both cases the RSA public key, made of a modulus and a public exponent, MUST be encoded using the RSAPublicKey type, and that encoding is carried in the certificate subject public key.

For the signature itself, the identifier is id-RSASSA-PSS too, and its parameters field MUST contain RSASSA-PSS-params. When signing, the RSA algorithm generates a single value, and that value is used directly as the signature value.
sections.eli5: Every key and every signature carries a small label saying which kind of math it uses. This section lists which labels are allowed and what extra notes must be attached to them.

sections.title: Signed-data Conventions and Validation
sections.content:
In signed-data, digestAlgorithms SHOULD contain the one-way hash function used to compute the message digest on the eContent value. The same hash function SHOULD be used for the digest on both eContent and signedAttributes, if signed attributes exist. That hash function MUST also be the one named as hashAlgorithm in the RSASSA-PSS parameters.

signatureAlgorithm MUST contain id-RSASSA-PSS with RSASSA-PSS-params as its parameters, and signature holds the single value from the signing operation.

If the certificate's public key uses id-RSASSA-PSS and its parameters field is present, a verifier MUST also check four things:

  • hashAlgorithm is the same in the certificate and in the signature parameters.
  • maskGenAlgorithm is the same in both.
  • saltLength in the signature parameters is greater than or equal to the one in the certificate.
  • trailerField is the same in both.

Default values count as equal to explicitly present values in these comparisons. If any of the four checks fails, the signature checking algorithm MUST fail validation.
sections.eli5: The certificate says what kind of seal its owner is allowed to use. The checker compares that with the seal on the message, and if anything does not match, or the salt is shorter than allowed, the message is rejected.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the RSA private key, since its compromise may allow signatures to be forged. Key generation relies on random numbers, and inadequate pseudo-random number generators can result in little or no security. The RFC points to RFC 1750 for guidance.

Using the same private key for different algorithms may let an attacker learn extra information about the key, so it is strongly suggested that the same key not be used for both PKCS #1 v1.5 and RSASSA-PSS. The same hash function should be used for all operations in a signature, which reduces the number of failure points.

The parameter checks in the signed-data section are of special importance, because it is possible to forge signatures by changing these parameter values, especially to weaker ones. Signers should use only one set of parameter values.
sections.eli5: Keep your seal stamp safe and make it from truly random material. Do not use the same stamp for two different kinds of seal, and always check that the seal matches what the certificate promises.
